title-group.article-title: When resilience is not enough: 2022 extreme marine heatwave threatens climatic refugia for a habitat‐forming Mediterranean octocoral

list-item.p: Climate change is impacting ecosystems worldwide, and the Mediterranean Sea is no exception. Extreme climatic events, such as marine heat waves (MHWs), are increasing in frequency, extent and intensity during the last decades, which has been associated with an increase in mass mortality events for multiple species.

Coralligenous assemblages, where the octocoral Paramuricea clavata lives, are strongly affected by MHWs. The Medes Islands Marine Reserve (NW Mediterranean) was considered a climate refugia for P. clavata, as their populations were showing some resilience to these changing conditions.
In this study, we assessed the impacts of the MHWs that occurred between 2016 and 2022 in seven shallow populations of the octocoral P. clavata from a Mediterranean Marine Protected Area.

The years that the mortality rates increased significantly were associated with the ones with strong MHWs, 2022 being the one with higher mortalities. In 2022, with 50 MHW days, the proportion of total affected colonies was almost 70%, with a proportion of the injured surface of almost 40%, reaching levels never attained in our study site since the monitoring was started.
We also found spatial variability between the monitored populations. Whereas few of them showed low levels of mortality, others lost around 75% of their biomass.

The significant impacts documented here raise concerns about the future of shallow P. clavata populations across the Mediterranean, suggesting that the resilience of this species may not be maintained to sustain these populations face the ongoing warming trends.

abstract.p: We are convinced that this paper can contribute to a better comprehension of the impact of climate change on marine ecosystems. We describe how Marine Heat Waves, which have been increasing in frequency, extent and intensity during the last decades, can negatively affect habitat‐forming species over time.

list-item.p: El canvi climatic està impactant els ecosistemes arreu del planeta, i el Mar Mediterrani no n'és una excepció. Els esdeveniments climàtics extrems, com ara les onades de calor marines, estan augmentant en freqüència, extensió i intensitat en les darreres dècades, i estan sent associades a un increment dels esdeveniments de mortalitat massiva de múltiples espècies.

El coral·ligen, on hi viu l'octocorall Paramuricea clavata, està altament afectat per les onades de calor marines. La Reserva Marina de les Illes Medes (NO del Mediterrani) es considerava un refugi climàtic per aquesta espècie, degut a que les seves poblacions mostraven certa resiliència a les condicions canviants.

En aquest estudi hem avaluat els impactes de les onades de calor marines succeïdes entre els anys 2016 i 2022 a set poblacions someres de l'octocorall P. clavata, en una Àrea Marina Protegida del Mediterrani.

Els anys en els quals les taxes de mortalitat van incrementar significativament s'associen amb els anys amb fortes onades de calor marines, sent el 2022 l'any amb la mortalitat més elevada. Al 2022, amb 50 dies d'onada de calor, la proporció total de colònies afectades va ser prop del 70%, amb un percentatge de superfície afectada de gairebé el 40%, arribant a valors mai observats en el lloc d'estudi des de que es va iniciar el seguiment d'aquestes poblacions.
També hem observat variabilitat espacial entre les poblacions mostrejades. Mentre que algunes d'elles han mostrat poca mortalitat, altres han perdut al voltant del 75% de la seva biomassa.

Els impactes documentats en aquest estudi mostren un futur preocupant de les poblacions someres de P. clavata arreu del Mediterrani, i això suggereix que la resiliència d'aquesta espècie podria no ser suficient per mantenir les seves poblacions en l'escenari d'escalfament que es preveu.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Climate change is emerging as one of the most pressing threats to global biodiversity (Bellard et al., 2012; Parmesan, 2006; Pereira et al., 2010). In marine ecosystems, it causes multiple impacts, such as acidification (Guinotte & Fabry, 2008) or sea level rise (Nicholls & Cazenave, 2010), but warming temperatures are particularly worrying (Oliver et al., 2018; Smale & Wernberg, 2013). Of particular concern are Marine heatwaves (MHWs), defined as discrete prolonged anomalously warm water events in a particular location (Hobday et al., 2016), which have already caused severe mortality events in benthic ecosystems worldwide, such as kelp forests (Wernberg et al., 2016) and coral reefs (Hughes et al., 2017, 2018), pushing them to the brink of collapse. Even more worrying is the fact that these events are expected to increase in frequency, intensity, duration and geographic extent in the coming decades (Darmaraki et al., 2019; Frölicher et al., 2018). Notwithstanding the widespread ecological disruptions caused by these catastrophic events, certain regions have shown resilience to these impacts, maintaining their structure and functioning despite these sudden climatic events (Krumhansl et al., 2016; Verdura et al., 2021). Termed as climate refugia by Keppel et al. (2012), these regions encompass habitats where components of biodiversity retreat to, persist in and can potentially expand from under changing environmental conditions. Therefore, understanding the consequences of these increasingly frequent climatic events, and the potential loss of climatic refugia, is the first necessary step to predict the future of marine ecosystems.

The Mediterranean Sea is one of the regions most affected by rising temperatures, with an average warming rate three times higher than the global average (IPCC et al., 2019). Its fast warming makes the Mediterranean Sea an outstanding model for studying the ecological consequences of climate change on marine biodiversity (Cramer et al., 2018). During the last decade, the frequency of MHW events has strongly increased in the Western Mediterranean Basin (Pastor & Khodayar, 2022), causing mass mortality events (MME) of many sessile benthic species (Garrabou, Gómez‐Gras, et al., 2022). The Mediterranean Sea is a hot spot of marine biodiversity, having one of the most unique habitats in terms of species richness and structural complexity, but also one of the most impacted by climate change, the coralligenous assemblages (Ballesteros, 2006; Garrabou, Gómez‐Gras, et al., 2022; Gómez‐Gras, Linares, Dornelas, et al., 2021). The octocorals are among the most affected species by mass mortality events, in particular, the red gorgonian Paramuricea clavata (Garrabou, Gómez‐Gras, et al., 2022). Most of these species display slow population dynamics with low mortality and recruitment rates (Garrabou & Harmelin, 2002; Linares et al., 2007) and limited dispersal capabilities (Pilczynska et al., 2016). These life‐history traits make them particularly vulnerable to climate change and MHWs (Garrabou, Gómez‐Gras, et al., 2022). In addition, most of these species have an important structural role, fostering the biodiversity of coralligenous habitats (Gómez‐Gras, Linares, Dornelas, et al., 2021; Ponti et al., 2018). Therefore, focusing on these habitat‐forming species together with the study of the impacts of climate change in the Mediterranean Sea will provide a window into the future for other regions worldwide.

In this study, we showcase the strong impacts of the MHW that took place during the 2022 summer on the Mediterranean benthic ecosystems. The extreme temperature conditions of summer 2022 made it one of the warmest summers ever registered in this region (Guinaldo et al., 2023), with MHWs lasting 50 days across the NW Mediterranean (www.t‐mednet.org, www.mercator‐ocean.eu). These MHWs mainly affect shallow populations (down to 30 m depth) due to the formation of the thermocline during the summer (Garrabou et al., 2009; Linares et al., 2005). Here, we compare the population status of the red gorgonian P. clavata with data from previous years (up to 7 years) in the Medes Islands Marine Reserve (NW Mediterranean). The P. clavata populations from this small Marine Reserve displayed resistance against previous MHWs that adversely affected other regions within the NW Mediterranean Sea (Garrabou et al., 2009). Given that resistance together with recovery is a component of resilience (Capdevila et al., 2020; Côté & Darling, 2010), previous results suggested that these populations were resilient to past MHWs and can be considered as a climate refugia (Garrabou et al., 2009; Linares, Coma, Garrabou, et al., 2008). We focus on the red gorgonian P. clavata because of its significant ecological value as a foundational species in the coralligenous habitats (Linares, Coma, Garrabou, et al., 2008). If MHWs keep increasing in the coming years, the future of these populations, and their associated biodiversity, at shallow depths will most likely disappear (Gómez‐Gras, Linares, López‐Sanz, et al., 2021; Verdura et al., 2019).

sec.title: Study site
sec.p: This study was performed at the Medes Islands Marine Reserve, located within the Montgrí, Illes Medes and Baix Ter Natural Park (NW Mediterranean Sea), with the approval of the Catalan Government under the project PTOP2017‐130 and PTOP‐2021‐3. The Marine Reserve was created in November 1983, when fishing activities were prohibited, becoming a No‐Take Protected Area. Some recreational activities are regulated within its boundaries, such as scuba diving or snorkelling, while activities like fishing or anchoring are banned. Also, there is a small island, Medallot, where only scientific scuba diving is allowed. In 2010, the government of Catalonia created the Montgrí, Medes Islands and Baix Ter Natural Park, encompassing the previously existing No‐Take Area.

sec.title: Population data and analyses
sec.p: We monitored seven populations of P. clavata over 7 years (from 2016 to 2022) during September and October, the months immediately after the summer period when the highest temperatures of the year have already occurred, and mortality caused by thermal stress is easily observable (Linares et al., 2010). At each population, we randomly placed a minimum of 30 quadrats (50 × 50 cm) between 15 and 20 m depth and then measured different parameters of each colony found within each quadrat: (i) the maximum height, directly measured with a ruler, (ii) the proportion of dead tissue, visually estimated relative to the total surface of the colony, and (iii) the mortality type: recent mortality (when the denuded axes of the gorgonians were clearly exposed or with remains of dead tissue), or old mortality (when the axis was epiphytized by algae, polychaetes or other organisms; Linares et al., 2005). To carry out this monitoring, we did not require ethics approval as it is a non‐invasive monitoring method.

With all the above information, we estimated different metrics to study the conservation status of the populations: (i) proportion of affected colonies each year (we considered an affected colony when the proportion of injured tissue exceeded 10% of the total gorgonian surface; Garrabou et al., 2009; Linares, Coma, & Zabala, 2008), (ii) mean proportion of affected surface per colony and (iii) proportion of biomass change from the start of the study (2016). To calculate the biomass (g of dry weight) first, we estimated the total biomass of the colonies using the adjusted relationship from Coma et al. (1998): b=0.002*h2.61 (where h is the maximum height, in cm). This biomass is corrected by subtracting the proportion of the total dead tissue of the colonies (Linares, Coma, & Zabala, 2008; Zentner et al., 2023). The dead tissue was visually estimated compared with the total surface of each colony as described above.

Finally, with these calculations, we analysed the temporal and spatial patterns of variation of P. clavata populations. For the temporal analyses, we calculated the mean values and standard error of the proportion of affected colonies (%) and the proportion of the total injured surface (%) across all sampled quadrats of the different populations each year of the study period. For the spatial analyses, we used two approximations: (i) the mean values of the proportion of affected colonies in the quadrats for each population for the year 2022 and (ii) the difference in the proportion of the mean quadrat biomass between the first (2016) and the last (2022) year of the study.

sec.title: Temperature data and analyses
sec.p: The temperature data used in this study were taken from the T‐MEDNet database, a collaborative initiative which conducts large‐scale and long‐term monitoring throughout the Mediterranean Sea over the past two decades (www.t‐mednet.org). The data from this repository were obtained by deploying HOBO data loggers that take high‐frequency (every hour) temperature data (accuracy ±0.21°C) from 0 to 40 m depth, every 5 m. Specifically, we used data from the data loggers deployed since 2002 at the Pota del Llop site (42° 2′ 58.920″ N, 3° 13′ 31.440″ E), situated within the Medes Islands Marine Reserve. Also, we selected the data from 15 m depth, where most of the studied populations were closest.

To analyse the temperature data and identify MHWs, we followed the analyses from Gómez‐Gras, Linares, Dornelas, et al. (2021). First, we identified the warmer period of the year. That is, the period comprised from the 1st of June to the 30th of November (JJASON period). Secondly, we calculated the days at which the populations were exposed to MHWs. We considered a MHW event as a discrete prolonged period of abnormally high seawater temperatures (>90th percentile of the in‐situ climatology) that lasted at least five consecutive days (Hobday et al., 2016). In this case, we considered the climatology period the available temperature data from 2002 until 2015. Also, we added the thermotolerance response for P. clavata at different temperatures and time exposures, previously calculated by Gómez‐Gras, Linares, Dornelas, et al. (2021), determining the onset of thermal stress for this particular species. Finally, to study the impact of exposure to high temperatures on these organisms, we used the: (i) intensity of exposure, being the highest temperature reached during MHWs, and (ii) the duration of the exposure, as the cumulative number of consecutive MHW days in a year (Bensoussan et al., 2019; Gómez‐Gras, Linares, Dornelas, et al., 2021). This method implies that the red gorgonian's vulnerability to impacts depends on these two factors. For instance, colonies may be exposed to high temperatures exceeding their tolerance limits, but if the duration of the event is short, they may not be significantly affected. Alternatively, even if the temperature is not excessively high, prolonged exposure to it can still lead to detrimental effects on the red gorgonian.

sec.title: Temporal analyses
sec.p: According to our defined criteria, over the period from 2016 to 2022, we identified four MHWs that surpassed the limits of thermotolerance of P. clavata in our study site, which took place in 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2022 (Figure 1a). Our results highlight that the 2022 MHW was the most severe, with a total of 50 days of MHWs registered and an intensity of 25.1°C (Figure 1a), affecting 68.2% (±2.19) of the colonies (Figure 1b), and a total mean of injured surface per colony of 38.2% (±1.08; Figure 1c). Also, we found a clear trend in the mortality indicators (cumulative proportion of affected colonies and injured surface) of the red gorgonian P. clavata, associated with the years with higher values of MHW days and intensity registered (stronger MHWs). For instance, during the years in which the values of MHWs (MHW days and intensity) were recorded as higher than P. clavata tolerates (i.e. 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2022, with 28, 42, 22 and 50 MHW days, respectively, and maximum temperatures above 24.3°C), there was a significant increase in both the proportion of affected colonies and the surface of individuals affected. On the contrary, in the years with values of MHW days and intensity within the thermotolerance range of our study species (i.e. 2016, 2020 and 2021, with maximum temperatures of 24.1°C, but only 12, 17 and 25 MHW days), the proportion of affected colonies and injured tissue were lower (Figure 1b,c). Furthermore, the years exhibiting stronger MHWs were also the ones showing higher mortalities: 2018 experienced 42 days of MHWs, which was the first year that, not only the proportion of affected colonies exceeded 50% (Figure 1b), but also the injured surface was above 20%, reaching 27.4% (Figure 1c). These results represent the average annual data across all seven populations.

caption.p: Temporal trends in different indicators of gorgonian mortality and marine heat waves (MHWs). (a) MHWs occurred over the years of the study, the circles represent MHWs detected, and their position represents the maximum exposure temperature (intensity), represented by the y‐axis, in relation to MHW days (duration), represented by the x‐axis. The size of the circles is proportional to their standardized position in the x‐ and y‐axis, meaning that higher temperatures exposed to more MHW days will be bigger and lower temperatures exposed to fewer MHW days will be smaller. The dashed line represents the thermotolerance response of Paramuricea clavata (calculated by Gómez‐Gras, Linares, Dornelas, et al., 2021); that means that the circles below the line, in blue, represent no harm for the colonies, and the circles above, in orange, can produce mortality due to severe MHWs. (b) Proportion of affected colonies (%) (colonies displaying >10% of the surface injured) each year of the study; the dots are the total mean of the proportion of colonies affected per year, while the error bar represents the standard error. (c) Proportion of the injured surface (%) each year of the study; the dots are the total mean of the proportion of injured surface per year, while the error bar represents the standard error. The circles represent the MHWs detected each year, and their size is the same as in (a), proportional to the MHW's intensity.

sec.title: Spatial analyses
sec.p: We found clear differences across the spatial scale of the study, with different populations being affected to different degrees. On the one hand, some populations, such as La Vaca and Pota del Llop, showed less than 50% of affected colonies (Figure 2a), while all the other populations showed a higher proportion (Figure 2a). In particular, Pedra de Déu, Tascó Petit, Tascó Gros and Carall Bernat, showed the highest partial mortality rates, with up to 93% of affected colonies (Figure 2a). Similarly, there was a clear spatial distinction in biomass loss (the total difference in biomass between 2016 and 2022), with La Vaca having a biomass increase (2%) and Pota del Llop showing a slight decrease (8%), while all other populations experienced a biomass decrease from 40% to 76% since 2016 (Figure 2b).

caption.p: Spatial distribution of the marine heat wave (MHW) impact on Paramuricea clavata. (a) Proportion of affected colonies at each population of the study during the year 2022. The colours represent the affection of the colonies: orange is the affected colonies and blue is the ones not affected (having less than 10% of the tissue injured). The red point marks the location of the HOBO data logger, at the Pota del Llop site (www.t‐mednet.org). (b) Proportion of biomass change between the first (2016) and the last year of the study (2022). Colours show if the population gained biomass (positive values, in blue), or lost biomass (negative values, in orange).

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: Our study highlights the adverse effects of extreme MHWs on Mediterranean gorgonians, with a particular focus on the 2022 event. Throughout our study, extreme climatic events have occurred as MHWs in our study area, but the last one (2022) was the most extreme ever registered there (Estaque et al., 2023; Garrabou, Zabala, et al., 2022; Marie et al., 2023). Here, we show that the persistent high temperatures during 2022 have resulted in an unprecedented increase in the mortality of the red gorgonian P. clavata in the Medes Islands Marine Reserve surveyed populations. These outcomes are quite alarming and threaten the viability of this gorgonian species at shallow depths.

Over the last decades, the Mediterranean Sea has experienced several thermal anomalies (Ibrahim et al., 2021), impacting many benthic species (Garrabou, Gómez‐Gras, et al., 2022). Some studies have shown high mortalities of gorgonians due to MHWs in the past, such as the one in 1999 in the Ligurian Sea with a proportion of affected colonies between 60% and 100% (Cerrano et al., 2000), or in 2003, with a value of an 80% in the Gulf of Genoa and Gulf of Naples (Garrabou et al., 2009). Despite the negative consequences of MHWs, some areas appeared to be acting as a climate refuge, where some species still resisted these extreme climatic events. Indeed, our study area acted as a haven where we could find large and well‐preserved populations of gorgonians, despite the effects of global warming (Coma et al., 2004; Linares, Coma, Garrabou, et al., 2008). In Medes Islands Marine Reserve, the occurrence of MHWs, such as the one in 2003, had less impact on coralligenous species than in other regions within the Mediterranean basin, probably due to the hydrodynamic conditions of the region and/or the adaptation to warmer conditions in comparison to the northern populations (Garrabou et al., 2009). Because human activities are regulated in our study site, it limits the impact of other stressors beyond MHWs, such as fishing or anchoring, except for diving activity, which has been recently demonstrated to have a synergistic effect with MHWs (Zentner et al., 2023). However, our findings suggest that the 2022 MHW might have triggered a tipping point for the populations of this species in this site, leading them towards extinction.

Despite the potential for extinction of these populations, the spatial patterns of mortality revealed a diversity of responses to MHWs among the monitored populations. Even though our study area is small (93 ha), it exhibits a diverse array of environmental conditions that could explain the differences among the studied populations. There are abiotic factors, such as sedimentation or water movement (Lenihan et al., 2008), that can differ even at small spatial scales, with potential beneficial or detrimental effects for organisms (Montero‐Serra et al., 2019; Zentner et al., 2023). For instance, some studies in tropical corals have shown that water circulation affects bleaching, either diminishing it and enhancing recovery (Anthony & Kerswell, 2007; Fabricius, 2006; Lenihan et al., 2008) or increasing it (McClanahan et al., 2005). In addition, in Mediterranean octocoral species, biotic factors such as population genetics (Crisci et al., 2017; Pilczynska et al., 2016), inter/intra‐specific competition (Linares, Coma, & Zabala, 2008; Ponti et al., 2014) and food availability (Coma et al., 2009) can also play a critical role in shaping the response of organisms to environmental perturbations. Because of these factors, and notwithstanding the small‐scale spatial distribution of our populations, the heterogeneous responses of the studied populations to MHWs would further support that some populations could have adaptative potential to warmer conditions (Gómez‐Gras et al., 2022) and they could act as a source for future repopulation of these species if environmental conditions were to improve. Nonetheless, recolonization is expected to be low in this species (Aurelle et al., 2020; Mokhtar‐Jamaï et al., 2011) with a strong spatial genetic structure due to their restricted connectivity (Arizmendi‐Mejia et al., 2015).

Overall, our study shows an unprecedented mortality event of P. clavata at the Medes Islands Marine Reserve, where the populations seemed to withstand high temperatures until the summer of 2022. While MME of the red gorgonian have been reported previously in the Mediterranean (Cerrano et al., 2000; Garrabou et al., 2009; Gómez‐Gras, Linares, López‐Sanz, et al., 2021; Iborra et al., 2022; Zentner et al., 2023), none showed the magnitude reached during 2022 at the NW Mediterranean Sea. The loss of these habitat‐forming species may trigger a reduction in the resilience of the whole ecosystem, as they have a primary role in mitigating physical and biological stress for associated fauna (Angelini et al., 2011; de la Torriente et al., 2020; Gómez‐Gras, Linares, López‐Sanz, et al., 2021). Therefore, at shallow depths, the associated biodiversity of these communities will likely be affected (Gómez‐Gras et al., 2019; Verdura et al., 2019). The unprecedented rise of global sea temperatures (Birkel, n.d.), together with the observed increase in frequency and intensity of MHWs, surpassing previous records, implies that existing projections may underestimate the potential ecological consequences of global warming on marine ecosystems.
